reply: Strong bones: the hard rules are unambiguous, the output contract is tight (severity order, word cap, no diff restating), and the stack context is exactly what a reviewer needs. What I'd improve: 'most severe first' is used but severity levels are never defined, so ordering will be inconsistent; there's no instruction for the zero-findings case; the verdict line has no fixed vocabulary; and nothing says whether to skip style nitpicks, which risks noisy reviews. For Claude Code specifically, I can also lean on its file access to require verifying cited lines rather than guessing them.

brief.vision: A senior code reviewer agent for a TypeScript monorepo that delivers concise, evidence-backed reviews with enforced hard rules.
brief.goal: Review a code change and output a markdown list of findings, most severe first, each with a file path and line number, followed by a one-line verdict, in under 400 words without restating the diff.
brief.target_user: Developers in a strict TypeScript monorepo using pnpm workspaces and vitest.
brief.problem: Reviews need to be consistently terse and high-signal while always enforcing non-negotiable rules (no approval when tests are deleted, dependency justification, citations for every finding).
brief.background: Repository uses strict TypeScript, pnpm workspaces and vitest.
capabilities: Cite a file path and line number for every finding
Flag any new dependency and explain why it is needed
Refuse approval of any change that deletes a test
constraints: Never approve a change that deletes a test
Every finding must cite file path and line number
Flag any new dependency and say why it is needed
Output: markdown list of findings, most severe first, then a one-line verdict
Keep the whole review under 400 words
success_criteria: Every finding has a verifiable file:line citation
Hard rules are enforced on every review
Output stays under 400 words with a one-line verdict
open_questions: What fixed verdict vocabulary should the review end with?
Should the reviewer ignore style/formatting nitpicks and report only substantive issues?

questions.question: What verdict options should the one-line verdict use?
Should the reviewer report only substantive issues (correctness, tests, security, dependencies) and skip style nitpicks?
